extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of poetics, drama, and classical literature; poets and dramatists interested in poetic theory
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and composing epic and tragic poetry (choice of metre, use of the wonderful/irrational, diction, unity, errors and their justification, and the comparative merits of tragedy and epic). Intended as theoretical rules and critical standards for poets and critics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of metre
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘the heroic measure has proved its fitness by the test of experience. If a narrative poem in any other metre or in many metres were now composed, it would be found incongruous.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The heroic is the stateliest and the most massive; it most readily admits rare words and metaphors. Iambic and trochaic tetrameter are stirring (trochaic akin to dancing, iambic expressive of action). Mixing different metres is absurd. 'Nature herself... teaches the choice of the proper measure.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet's self-presentation (narratorial intrusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The poet should speak as little as possible in his own person, for it is not this that makes him an imitator.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good poet lets the characters speak and imitates them; Homer speaks little in his own person, bringing characters directly on stage. Avoid appearing oneself upon the scene (anti-pattern: frequent authorial intrusions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinct characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should be 'none of them wanting in characteristic qualities, but each with a character of his own.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When introducing a personage, give them characteristic qualities so they are individually recognizable and consistent; avoid flat or indistinct characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the wonderful (element of the marvelous)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The element of the wonderful is required in Tragedy. The irrational, on which the wonderful depends for its chief effects, has wider scope in Epic poetry, because there the person acting is not seen... The wonderful is pleasing.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The marvelous/irrational may be employed for poetic effect (example: Odyssey Bath Scene). In epic the audience imagines unseen actions so absurdities pass unnoticed; on stage such absurdities may be ludicrous. Use wonder where it enhances effect, but be wary of stage visibility and plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer probable impossibilities to improbable possibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The poet should prefer probable impossibilities to improbable possibilities. The tragic plot must not be composed of irrational parts.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid irrational elements within the action; if impossible or irrational elements are necessary they should be made probable (an 'air of likelihood') or placed outside the dramatic action (e.g., a hero's ignorance). Do not construct a plot dependent on irrational incidents unless they can be justified; the plea that 'otherwise the plot would have been ruined' is ridiculous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement and degree of diction
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The diction should be elaborated in the pauses of the action, where there is no expression of character or thought. For, conversely, character and thought are merely obscured by a diction that is over brilliant.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve ornate or elaborate language for pauses and sections without active characterization; during moments of character-expression or thought prefer clarity over brilliance. Avoid overwrought diction that obscures character or meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects imitated (threefold classification)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The poet being an imitator... must of necessity imitate one of three objects — things as they were or are, things as they are said or thought to be, or things as they ought to be.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging poetic representation, identify which of the three modes the poet is imitating (actual fact, common belief/report, or idealized form) and assess appropriateness of language and representation accordingly; the vehicle of expression may be current terms or rare words/metaphors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of correctness differs by art; essential vs accidental faults
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘the standard of correctness is not the same in poetry and politics... Within the art of poetry itself there are two kinds of faults,—those which touch its essence, and those which are accidental.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between errors inherent to the poetic art (e.g., failure in imitation due to lack of capacity) and accidental technical inaccuracies (e.g., mistaken technical detail in medicine, horsemanship). The former are more serious to judgment of the poem than the latter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justification of impossible descriptions by artistic ends
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘If he describes the impossible, he is guilty of an error; but the error may be justified, if the end of the art be thereby attained... If, however, the end might have been as well, or better, attained without violating the special rules of the poetic art, the error is not justified.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An impossible or untrue depiction can be permitted if it produces the artistic effect intended and could not be achieved otherwise; if the same effect could be achieved without violating poetic rules, then the impossibility is unjustified. Strive to avoid errors when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Severity of errors depends on whether they touch essentials
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: ‘not to know that a hind has no horns is a less serious matter than to paint it inartistically.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate mistakes by their impact on the essence of the art: factual slips that do not harm poetic effect are less serious than errors that make the imitation unartistic or implausible in its core.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual criteria for judging acts or sayings
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘we must not look merely to the particular act or saying... We must also consider by whom it is said or done, to whom, when, by what means, or for what end.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess lines and actions in their dramatic context (speaker, audience, timing, means, purpose). An act/saying may be right or wrong poetically depending on these circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve difficulties by attention to language usage (metaphor, dialect, accent, punctuation, ambiguity)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Other difficulties may be resolved by due regard to the usage of language. We may note a rare word... It is not meant that his body was ill-shaped, but that his face was ugly... It is not meant... “mix the drink livelier”...’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a passage seems problematic, consider: rare/local meanings, metaphors, regional usages, accent/breathing, punctuation, ambiguity of words, and conventional uses (e.g., calling mixed drink 'wine'). Use linguistic and cultural knowledge to interpret passages before judging them erroneous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation guided by poet's own usage and tacit assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The true mode of interpretation is the precise opposite of what Glaucon mentions... The question... should be solved by reference to what the poet says himself, or to what is tacitly assumed by a person of intelligence.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid hasty critical inferences; prefer interpretations consistent with the poet's wording and what a reasonable, intelligent reader would tacitly assume; beware critics who 'jump at certain groundless conclusions.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Justifying impossibility by artistic requirements, higher reality, or received opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘the impossible must be justified by reference to artistic requirements, or to the higher reality, or to received opinion. With respect to the requirements of art, a probable impossibility is to be preferred to a thing improbable and yet possible.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow impossible elements when they serve artistic ideals (the ideal may surpass reality), when they fit accepted belief or convention, or when they help achieve the art's ends; prefer 'probable impossibility' (plausible within art) to mere unlikely actuality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine apparent contradictions by dialectical rules
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Things that sound contradictory should be examined by the same rules as in dialectical refutation—whether the same thing is meant, in the same relation, and in the same sense.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To reconcile contradictions, test whether terms are being used in different senses/relations; prioritize poet's intended meaning or the reasonable tacit assumption to resolve apparent inconsistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censure irrationality or moral depravity only when unnecessary
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The element of the irrational, and, similarly, depravity of character, are justly censured when there is no inner necessity for introducing them.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irrational incidents or morally bad characterizations should be criticized if there is no internal, dramatic reason for them. Examples: introduction of Aegeus by Euripides, or badness of Menelaus in the Orestes are censured for lack of necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five sources of critical objection
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Things are censured either as impossible, or irrational, or morally hurtful, or contradictory, or contrary to artistic correctness.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When addressing criticism, categorize objections under these five headings and seek answers using the various interpretive heads (linguistic, dialectical, appeal to artistic necessity, received opinion, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish poetic art from histrionic/performance faults
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘this censure attaches not to the poetic but to the histrionic art; for gesticulation may be equally overdone in epic recitation... Tragic art, then, as a whole, stands to Epic in the same relation as the younger to the elder actors.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate poor stage performance (bad gesticulation, overacting) with defects of the poem itself. Critique performance separately from poetic composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for comparing Tragedy and Epic (unity, concentration, audience, vividness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy attains its end within narrower limits; the concentrated effect is more pleasurable than one spread over long time. Epic imitation has less unity; tragedies are more concentrated and can achieve a more perfect imitation of a single action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate genres by their capacity to attain their specific ends: tragedy's concentrated, unified action often produces a higher, purer effect than epic's length and multiplicity of actions. Examples: Oedipus would be weakened if made as long as the Iliad; epic poems may furnish subjects for several tragedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and single-action imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘<Such length implies some loss of unity,> if, I mean, the poem is constructed out of several actions, like the Iliad and the Odyssey... each is... an imitation of a single action.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good poem (especially tragic) should imitate a single action with appropriate magnitude; constructing a poem out of several actions risks loss of unity and dilution of effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music and spectacle as important accessories
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘music and spectacular effects as important accessories ; and these produce the most vivid of pleasures.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize music and spectacle as powerful supporting elements that enhance vividness and pleasure, but distinguish them as accessories to the poetic art rather than its primary constituents.
